You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

//! Command line interface definition.

use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgGroup, ArgMatches, Command};

const AFTER_HELP: &str = "
If your .git directory is a child of your project directory (most common, such as /myproject/.git) AND not in the current working directory (i.e you need to use --work-tree or --git-dir) you only need to specify either the --work-tree (i.e. /myproject) OR --git-dir (i.e. /myproject/.git), you don't need to use both.

If using the --config to specify a clog configuration TOML file NOT in the current working directory (meaning you need to use --work-tree or --git-dir) AND the TOML file is inside your project directory (i.e. /myproject/.clog.toml) you do not need to use --work-tree or --git-dir.";

const ALL_ARGS: [&str; 17] = [
    "repository",
    "from",
    "format",
    "major",
    "git_dir",
    "work_tree",
    "minor",
    "patch",
    "subtitle",
    "to",
    "outfile",
    "config",
    "infile",
    "setversion",
    "from_latest_tag",
    "link_style",
    "changelog",
];

fn opt(id: &'static str, short: Option<char>, long: &'static str, value: &'static str) -> Arg {
    let mut a = Arg::new(id)
        .long(long)
        .value_name(value)
        .action(ArgAction::Set)
        .num_args(1)
        .required(false);
    if let Some(s) = short {
        a = a.short(s);
    }
    a
}

fn flag(id: &'static str, short: char, long: &'static str) -> Arg {
    Arg::new(id)
        .short(short)
        .long(long)
        .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
}

pub fn build() -> Command {
    Command::new("clog")
        .version("0.10.0")
        .about("a conventional changelog for the rest of us")
        .after_help(AFTER_HELP)
        .group(ArgGroup::new("Args").multiple(true).args(ALL_ARGS))
        .arg(
            opt("repository", Some('r'), "repository", "URL").help(
                "Repository used for generating commit and issue links (without the .git, e.g. https://github.com/thoughtram/clog)",

fn run(args: &cli::Args) -> error::Result<()> {
    let clog = clog::Clog::from_args(args)?;
    let commits = clog.get_commits()?;
    clog.write_changelog(commits)?;
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {

    let start = Instant::now();

impl Args {
    pub fn parse() -> Args {
        let raw: Vec<OsString> = std::env::args_os().collect();
        let mut cmd = build();
        let m = match cmd.try_get_matches_from_mut(raw.iter().cloned()) {
            Ok(m) => m,
            Err(mut e) => {
                if e.kind() == ErrorKind::UnknownArgument {
                    if let Some(ContextValue::String(invalid)) = e.get(ContextKind::InvalidArg).cloned() {
                        let suggested = match e.get(ContextKind::SuggestedArg) {
                            Some(ContextValue::String(s)) => Some(s.clone()),
                            _ => None,
                        };
                        let rest = &raw[1.min(raw.len())..];
                        if let Some(usage) = unknown_long_usage(&cmd, rest, &invalid, suggested.as_deref()) {
                            e.insert(ContextKind::Usage, ContextValue::StyledStr(usage));
                        }
                    }
                }
                e.exit()
            }
        };
        Args {
            repository: get_str(&m, "repository"),
            from: get_str(&m, "from"),
            format: get_str(&m, "format").unwrap_or_else(|| "markdown".to_string()),
            major: m.get_flag("major"),
            git_dir: get_str(&m, "git_dir"),
            work_tree: get_str(&m, "work_tree"),
            minor: m.get_flag("minor"),
            patch: m.get_flag("patch"),
            subtitle: get_str(&m, "subtitle"),
            to: get_str(&m, "to").unwrap_or_else(|| "HEAD".to_string()),
            outfile: get_str(&m, "outfile"),
            config: get_str(&m, "config").unwrap_or_else(|| ".clog.toml".to_string()),
            infile: get_str(&m, "infile"),
            setversion: get_str(&m, "setversion"),
            from_latest_tag: m.get_flag("from_latest_tag"),
            link_style: get_str(&m, "link_style").unwrap_or_else(|| "github".to_string()),
            changelog: get_str(&m, "changelog"),
        }
    }
}

/// Which arguments had been recorded when an unknown long flag was met.
#[derive(Default)]
struct Used {
    any: bool,
    setversion: bool,
}

impl Used {
    fn mark(&mut self, id: &str) {
        if ALL_ARGS.contains(&id) {
            self.any = true;
        }
        if id == "setversion" {
            self.setversion = true;
        }
    }
}

fn takes_value(arg: &Arg) -> bool {
    matches!(arg.get_action(), ArgAction::Set | ArgAction::Append)
}

fn is_value_token(tok: &str) -> bool {
    !(tok.starts_with('-') && tok != "-")
}

/// Rebuilds the usage line shown for an unknown `--long` argument: the
/// arguments parsed so far (and a suggested similar argument) are rendered
/// through the argument groups they belong to.  Returns `None` when the
/// default usage line applies.
fn unknown_long_usage(
    cmd: &Command,
    raw: &[OsString],
    invalid: &str,
    suggested: Option<&str>,
) -> Option<StyledStr> {
    if !invalid.starts_with("--") {
        return None;
    }

**How I checked it:** I ran both binaries in the same scenario and compared exit code, stdout, stderr and any files written, with the "took N ms" time and panic thread IDs blanked out. This covered:
- real git repos;
- a fake `git` on `PATH` that logs its arguments and returns made-up output;
- about 200 hand-written TOML configs;
- randomly generated configs, commit messages and command lines;
- help output at different terminal widths, with colours forced on, and on a real terminal.

**What it reproduces, including the original's bugs:**
- **Command line:** help, version, error messages and exit codes, including the odd "Usage:" line shown after a mistyped `--option`.
- **Config file:** it follows the original's lenient parser. For example, a repeated section name keeps the last value, and some invalid dates are accepted.
- **Settings that are read but have no effect:** `repository`, `subtitle`, `link-style`, `output-format`, `git-dir` and `git-work-tree` from the config are overridden by command-line values or defaults.
- **No built-in sections:** without a `[sections]` table no commits are listed, and `git log` always gets the same fixed, slightly broken `--grep` pattern.
- **Version bumps:** `-p`/`-m`/`-M` always fail against real git, because the tag name from git ends in a newline.
- **JSON output:** `None`/`Some("…")` written as-is, the subtitle unquoted, and `breaks` listing the closed issues.
- **Crashes:** the same crash messages, file paths and exit code 101, e.g. when a section uses the `unk` alias.
- **Other:** the date is always UTC, and everything (including "changelog written. (took N ms)") goes to stdout.

**Things to know:**
- **Build depends on the local cache.** The build uses `clap` 4.6.1, `regex` and `semver` from the machine's Cargo cache, pinned in `Cargo.lock`. `compile.sh` builds offline first and only tries downloading if that fails.
- **Small stand-in module.** Wrapping help text to the terminal width needs a small package (`terminal_size`) that wasn't in the cache, so I wrote my own small version in `shims/terminal_size`.
- **Workaround for a clap difference.** The original was built with an older clap that prints a different "Usage:" line after a mistyped long option. I rebuild that line myself in `src/cli.rs`.
- **Original binary moved.** To keep it for comparison I moved it to `/tmp/orig/executable`. `./executable` in the workspace is now the new build, and both it and `target/` are in `.gitignore`.

**Known gaps:**
- With `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` set, crash output won't match, because the original prints a stack trace.
- The "took N ms" figure is only roughly the same (both usually show about 2 ms).

I've rebuilt the tool in Rust, and it matched the original's output on every differential test I ran. Each test ran both binaries in identical scenarios and compared stdout, stderr, exit code and any files written. The work is committed, `./compile.sh` builds `./executable`, and a fresh clone builds offline.

**How I worked it out:**
- I only ran the binary and read the bundled docs; no decompiling or tracing.
- To see what it asks git, I put a logging `git` wrapper on `PATH`. The same wrapper could replay canned output, which let me test commit-parsing edge cases.
- Tests covered the help and error text (including terminal widths, `COLUMNS` and colour settings), config files, commit messages, links, markdown/JSON output and file handling. I also ran random-input fuzzing over config files, commit logs and argument lists, a few thousand cases with no differences left.

**Behaviours I copied on purpose, even though they look like bugs in the original:**
- The `git log --grep` pattern is always the built-in default and never reflects your config. And if the config has no `[sections]`, no commits are listed at all.
- In `.clog.toml`, `repository`, `subtitle`, `link-style` and `output-format` are read and type-checked but then ignored; only the command-line values count.
- `from-latest-tag` in the config runs `git` with empty directory arguments, so it finds nothing.
- `-p`/`-m`/`-M` always fail with real git, because the tag name keeps its trailing newline and doesn't parse as a version.
- The original crashes in a few cases (for example, any section using the alias `unk`). Mine crashes the same way, with the same message, source location and exit code 101.
- JSON quirks are kept: `"version":None` or `Some("…")`, the subtitle unquoted, and `breaks` repeating the `closes` list.
- Config parsing reproduces the original's lenient TOML reading (duplicate keys allowed with the last one winning, dates only loosely checked) rather than the strict standard.

**Dependencies:** the build uses `clap`, `regex` and `semver` from the local cargo registry cache, pinned in `Cargo.lock`. Matching the original's help wrapping needed a terminal-size crate that isn't in the cache, so I wrote a small replacement under `shims/terminal_size`. My `clap` is a slightly newer version than the original's. That changed one usage line shown for unknown `--long` options, and I patch that line myself.

**Limits:**
- The build depends on that local registry cache. Without it, `compile.sh` falls back to downloading, which needs internet.
- The "took N ms" figure can't be matched exactly. My timings come out similar (about 2 ms in tests).
- With `RUST_BACKTRACE` set, crash output won't match.

I moved the original binary to `/tmp/orig/executable` to compare against it. `./executable` is now my build and is git-ignored.
